titre: The Pact That Outlawed War Without Preventing It
accroche: On August 27, 1928, dozens of states promise never to wage war again. Eleven years later, three of them have started one.
contenu_vulgarise:
On August 27, 1928, in the Clock Room of the Quai d'Orsay, fifteen delegations sign a treaty of unusual brevity: three articles, barely a page. Its first article fits in one sentence: the parties “condemn recourse to war for the solution of international controversies, and renounce it, as an instrument of national policy in their relations with one another.” No exceptions, no definition of aggression, no enforcement mechanism: a promise, without the means to make it hold.

## From a bilateral proposal to sixty-three states

The text grows out of a more modest initiative. In April 1927, French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand proposes to the United States alone a bilateral pact renouncing war, ten years after America entered the war at France's side. Secretary of State Frank Kellogg answers by widening the proposal to all the great powers: a collective commitment, rather than a two-party alliance that might have looked like a pact aimed at a third country. The treaty enters into force on July 24, 1929, once the original signatories' ratifications have been deposited in Washington, and then opens to accession by other states. Within a few years, sixty-three of them have joined: nearly the entire international scene of the day, Germany, Italy and Japan included.

Yet the pact prevents neither Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931, nor Italy's invasion of Ethiopia in 1935, nor Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939: all three were signatories. No clause provided for any consequence if it was violated, and none of the three wars is even declared: it quickly becomes clear that a text that bans war without defining it simply lets its signatories stop calling it by name.

## A promise without force, turned into a charge

Still, the pact finds a use again at Nuremberg, in 1945. The International Military Tribunal sees in it proof that by 1939 wars of aggression were already forbidden by a text Germany had itself signed eleven years earlier: the “war in violation of international treaties,” covered by Article 6 of its charter among the crimes against peace, includes in particular a violation of the 1928 pact. A treaty that could prevent nothing thus becomes, eighteen years after its signing, one of the legal foundations of the gravest charge brought against the Nazi leaders: proof that they knew war was already outlawed.

carte.punch: In 1928, fifteen states sign the pact against war. Sixty-three joined it.
carte.idee: On August 27, 1928, fifteen delegations sign the Kellogg-Briand Pact in Paris, which sixty-three states join within a few years. It stops neither Manchuria (1931), nor Ethiopia (1935), nor Poland (1939), but in 1945 it is used to try those who had signed it.

quiz.question: Why does the 1928 Kellogg-Briand Pact, which stopped none of the major invasions of the 1930s, find a use again in 1945?
choix: Because Nuremberg sees in it proof that wars of aggression were already forbidden by a text signed by Germany itself
Because it already provided for the death penalty for any violation, applied for the first time in 1945
Because the Allies amended it in 1945 to add the sanctions it originally lacked
Because Germany had signed it a second time in 1939, just before invading Poland
quiz.explication: The pact provided no sanctions and was never amended after the fact: it is the very fact that Germany signed it in 1928 that the Nuremberg tribunal uses in 1945, to establish that the war it waged violated a commitment already made.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was Aristide Briand's initial proposal in April 1927, before Frank Kellogg widened it?
choix: A multilateral pact open to all the great powers from the start
A bilateral pact renouncing war, addressed to the United States alone
A defensive military alliance between France and Germany
A naval disarmament treaty limited to the French and American navies
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In April 1927 Briand proposed a bilateral pact with the United States alone; it was Kellogg who widened it into a collective commitment, to avoid a two-party alliance that might have seemed aimed at a third country.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many articles does the treaty signed on August 27, 1928 contain?
choix: Twenty-three articles, like the Treaty of Versailles
A single article, a mere statement of intent
Twelve articles divided into four chapters
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text fits in three articles, barely a page: a first article renouncing war, a second on the peaceful settlement of disputes, a third on entry into force on July 24, 1929.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which three signatories of the pact nonetheless launched an invasion in the 1930s?
choix: The United Kingdom, France and the Netherlands
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, Italy Ethiopia in 1935, and Germany Poland in 1939; all three were signatories of the pact, and none of these wars was officially declared.
